title: The Trial Record and the Close-Up: Dreyer from Vor Frue to Frederiksberg
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Vor Frue parish, Copenhagen: the birth that is not kept
stops.date_confidence: attested; Dansk Biografisk Leksikon and the Danish Film Institute extended biography agree on date and parish
stops.campa: In the parish of Vor Frue, a Swedish housekeeper named Josefina Bernhardina Nielsson bears a son to the Danish landowner Jens Christian Torp, in whose house she works. The child is entered as Carl Theodor. He is illegitimate and he is not kept. His first two years pass in foster and orphanage care in Copenhagen while his mother goes on working. Nothing in the parish record, and nothing in Torp's later conduct, suggests another arrangement was ever considered. He is most of the way grown before anyone tells him any of it.
suggested_refs: The baptismal register of Vor Frue Kirke, Copenhagen, February 1889
sources: Danish Film Institute, 'Carl Th. Dreyer, Biography (extended)'

stops.name: Copenhagen: the typographer's household
stops.date_confidence: adoption attested by Dansk Biografisk Leksikon, which gives the adoptive parents' dates as 1864-1911 and 1863-1937; the exact date of adoption is not given and the day and month are defaulted. The household address is not named in any source reached and the pin is approximate.
stops.campa: The typographer Carl Theodor Dreyer and his wife Inger Marie adopt the boy and hand him the man's entire name. The house is frugal and the charity comes itemized. His adoptive grandmother lives with them and is the one he gets along with. What he remembers of the parents is an account book: the food was a favor, the favor was owed to nobody, and his mother had escaped the debt by lying down to die. He repeats their sentence about it half a century later without softening a syllable.
stops.quote: constantly let me know that I should be grateful for the food I was given and that I strictly had no claim on anything since my mother got out of paying by lying down to die.
stops.quote_source: Dreyer's recollection of his adoptive parents, Danish Film Institute, 'Carl Th. Dreyer, Biography (extended)'
suggested_refs: The Danish Film Institute's extended Dreyer biography, which preserves this recollection verbatim
sources: Danish Film Institute, 'Carl Th. Dreyer, Biography (extended)'

stops.name: Copenhagen: the mother dead at thirty-five
stops.date_confidence: death date and age attested by the Danish Film Institute extended biography; Dansk Biografisk Leksikon independently gives her dates as 1855-91. The phosphorus tradition itself is [R]: neither that biography nor the Leksikon states the method. The coordinate is a central-Copenhagen placeholder, since no address for the foster care or for her death is named in any source reached.
stops.campa: Josefina Nielsson dies on the twentieth of January, thirty-five years old. Tradition, carried down from Martin Drouzy's archival work, holds that she died trying to end a later pregnancy with phosphorus scraped from match heads; the institutional biographies record the death and the age and say nothing at all about the method. Her son is not yet two and is already living in another family's house under another family's name. What he will hear about her, years later, is a sentence in his adoptive parents' mouths about a woman who got out of paying. He keeps no memory of her face and none of her voice.
suggested_refs: Martin Drouzy's archival reconstruction of Dreyer's parentage, the source of the phosphorus tradition
sources: Danish Film Institute, 'Carl Th. Dreyer, Biography (extended)'

stops.name: Frederiksberg Realskole: the finals of 1904
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Danish Film Institute extended biography, which names both schools and the year of the finals; the month is not given and is defaulted
stops.campa: From the municipal school on Nansensgade his adoptive parents move him to the private Frederiksberg Realskole, a step up they can barely carry. Classmates remember a clever boy who kept himself to himself. Whatever he later knows about lenses, stock, cutting and the handling of a crew he will take off the job or out of books: there is no university ahead of him, and in 1904 there is no film school anywhere to go to instead. He sits his finals that year, at fifteen, and leaves the house not long afterward.
suggested_refs: The Frederiksberg Realskole examination rolls of 1904
sources: Danish Film Institute, 'Carl Th. Dreyer, Biography (extended)'

stops.name: Kongens Nytorv, the Great Northern Telegraph Company: the clerk who runs
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Danish Film Institute extended biography for both the September 1905 entry and the departure in early 1908; the Kongens Nytorv coordinate is a landmark-level approximation of the company's main office and is not confirmed by the fetched source
stops.campa: A short clerical stint at the Copenhagen utility company comes first, then in September 1905 the Great Northern Telegraph Company, the Danish concern whose cables run to Vladivostok and Shanghai. He files ledgers there for two and a half years. He will say later that the office years were his real education, and he means the arithmetic of it: a column balances or it does not, and no amount of feeling about the figures will move it. In early 1908 he walks out, horrified, by his own account, at the prospect of a lifetime of the work.
suggested_refs: The Great Northern Telegraph Company's Copenhagen headquarters, employer of the sixteen-year-old Dreyer
sources: Danish Film Institute, 'Carl Th. Dreyer, Biography (extended)'

stops.name: Berlingske Tidende, Copenhagen: the aviation desk
stops.date_confidence: the 1909 start at Berlingske Tidende is attested by Dansk Biografisk Leksikon; the aviation beat is attested by the Danish Film Institute extended biography. Month and day are not given and are defaulted. The street address of the offices is not confirmed by any source reached.
stops.campa: At twenty he gets into journalism at Berlingske Tidende, and the paper puts him on the newest beat in Europe. The writing of these years is compressed and unsentimental about detail, which is what a daily pays for. He covers the flying meetings, learns how the machines are rigged, takes lessons himself, and scoops the first flight across the Sound between Denmark and Sweden. Cinema does not come into it yet. He is a reporter on the aviation desk of a Copenhagen paper, twenty years old, learning how a thing works and how few words it takes to say so.
suggested_refs: Dreyer's aviation reportage in Berlingske Tidende, c. 1909-1911
sources: Danish Film Institute, 'Carl Th. Dreyer, Biography (extended)'

stops.name: Over the Oresund: first passenger on the crossing
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Danish Film Institute extended biography, which names the French aviator Poulain and the year 1911; month and day are not given and are defaulted. The coordinate is a strait-level proxy: no departure field and no landing site is named in any source reached. Note also that an earlier dossier line placed Dreyer's aviation work at the newspaper Riget and had him flying in balloons; no fetched source supports either, and the corrected reading is aeroplanes at Berlingske.
stops.campa: The French aviator Poulain flies the Sound between Denmark and Sweden and Dreyer is in the machine with him, the first passenger carried across on such a flight and the reporter filing his own story afterward. He is twenty-two years old. Nothing in the record suggests he understood the trip as preparation for anything, and nothing in the films he later makes looks back at it. Wood, wire and doped canvas over cold water, with the ferry lanes his countrymen have used for a thousand years running underneath.
suggested_refs: Contemporary Danish press accounts of the first Denmark-Sweden passenger flight, 1911
sources: Danish Film Institute, 'Carl Th. Dreyer, Biography (extended)'

stops.name: Copenhagen: the marriage, and the typographer's death
stops.date_confidence: marriage date attested by Dansk Biografisk Leksikon; the adoptive father's death in 1911 is attested by the same source, which gives his dates as 1864-1911, but the exact date is not given and the two events are placed at one pin. The children's birth years come from the English Wikipedia article.
stops.campa: On the nineteenth of November he marries Ebba Frederikke Larsen. The marriage runs fifty-seven years, until the day he dies, and leaves almost no mark in the enormous literature about him; a daughter, Gunni, arrives in 1913, a son, Erik, in 1923. The same year as the wedding his adoptive father dies at forty-seven. The typographer who kept telling him he had no claim on anything is in the ground before the son has directed a frame. No source reached says whether Dreyer went to the funeral.
suggested_refs: The Copenhagen marriage register, 19 November 1911

stops.name: Ekstra Bladet, Copenhagen: profiles with a knife in them
stops.date_confidence: the 1912 start at Ekstra Bladet is attested by Dansk Biografisk Leksikon; the Asta Nielsen profile is attested by the Danish Film Institute extended biography. Month and day defaulted. The coordinate is a central-Copenhagen placeholder; the paper's address is not named in any source reached. The Bryggerens Datter sale is [R], from composite filmographies only.
stops.campa: He writes for Ekstra Bladet: reportage, court reporting, and celebrity profiles with a knife inside them, one of them on Asta Nielsen, the Danish actress all of Europe is watching. He is also selling scenarios on the side, among them Bryggerens Datter to a small trading house dabbling in film. He works for the paper Riget in the same stretch. The man doing this is not a young radical of the arts. Asked about it much later, he places himself with some precision.
stops.quote: Even when I was with Ekstrabladet, I was conservative...I don't believe in revolutions.
stops.quote_source: Dreyer, quoted in David Bordwell, The Films of Carl Theodor Dreyer (University of California Press, 1983), p. 191
suggested_refs: Dreyer's Ekstra Bladet profile of Asta Nielsen
sources: Danish Film Institute, 'Carl Th. Dreyer, Biography (extended)'
Bordwell, The Films of Carl Theodor Dreyer (1983)

stops.name: Nordisk Films Kompagni, Valby: hired to read other men's stories
stops.date_confidence: attested by Dansk Biografisk Leksikon for the 1913 hiring and the count of roughly twenty-two filmed scripts to 1918; month and day defaulted. The 1915 premiere date for Ned med Vaabnene comes from the Danish Film Institute's Filmdatabasen, against the 1914 writing date given in composite filmographies.
stops.campa: Nordisk Films Kompagni, then one of the largest studios in the world, takes him on at Valby as scenario reader, screenwriter, and editor. Among the scripts is Ned med Vaabnene, from Bertha von Suttner's pacifist novel, filmed by Holger-Madsen and premiered in September 1915, a year into the war it argued against. He learns the apparatus from inside it, in the order a craftsman learns anything: what a story costs, what a set can be made to do, where a scene dies in the cutting room. Between 1913 and 1918 roughly twenty-two of his scripts are shot by other men.
suggested_refs: Ned med Vaabnene! (Holger-Madsen, Nordisk, premiered 18 September 1915), from Bertha von Suttner's Die Waffen nieder!
sources: Danish Film Institute Filmdatabasen, 'Ned med Vaabnene!'
Danish Film Institute, 'Carl Th. Dreyer, Biography (extended)'

stops.name: Gotland: the first film he directs himself
stops.date_confidence: [R] for Gotland: only the Danish Film Institute extended biography mentions the island, and the institute's own page for Praesidenten does not. The dates are contested three ways: the extended biography says he directed it in 1918, the film page gives production year 1919 with a Swedish premiere on 3 February 1919, and Dansk Biografisk Leksikon's 1920 is the Danish premiere at Panoptikon on 9 February. Not resolved here. The coordinate is Visby, an island-level proxy, not a documented shooting site.
stops.campa: He takes the camera himself for the first time, on Praesidenten, from a novel by Karl Emil Franzos, with location work on the Baltic island of Gotland. He is twenty-nine and has been reading other people's scenarios for five years. The film is finished by 1919 and Sweden sees it in February of that year; Copenhagen does not see it until February 1920. Two years after that comes Blade af Satans Bog, four episodes across two millennia, built openly on the architecture of Griffith's Intolerance, a film he has taken apart and studied.
suggested_refs: Praesidenten (Nordisk Films Kompagni), Swedish premiere 3 February 1919, Danish premiere 9 February 1920 at Panoptikon
Blade af Satans Bog (1921), after Griffith's Intolerance
sources: Danish Film Institute, 'Carl Th. Dreyer, Biography (extended)'

segments.name: Stave Church, Rented Studio, Foreign Money

stops.name: Garmo stave church, Maihaugen, Lillehammer: the parsonage assembled around the shoot
stops.date_confidence: attested: English Wikipedia's article on The Parson's Widow states that both exterior and interior shots were filmed at the Garmo Stave Church and the Maihaugen museum, for Svensk Filmindustri, released 4 October 1920. Month defaulted. Coordinate taken from the Garmo Stave Church article, correcting an earlier dossier value about a kilometre off.
stops.campa: For a Swedish production he shoots Praestaenkan at Maihaugen, in the open-air museum above Lillehammer, using the Garmo stave church and its farm buildings instead of built sets. The church is medieval, raised around 1150 on the site of an older one, and it is at this exact moment being taken apart and re-erected at Maihaugen; the reassembly runs through 1920 and 1921, the same seasons as the film. He is photographing a building in the act of being moved. The story, from Kristofer Janson, is a comedy about an old woman who outlives three husbands.
suggested_refs: Kristofer Janson's story 'Prestekonen', the film's literary source
The Garmo stave church, re-erected at Maihaugen 1920-1921

stops.name: Berlin, Primus-Film: the pogrom picture
stops.date_confidence: the 1922 German production of Die Gezeichneten and the casting of Jewish refugees are attested by Dansk Biografisk Leksikon; the Primus-Film connection is [R], from the Danish Film Institute extended biography, which names the company and the city but no address. The Berlin coordinate is city-level. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: In Germany he makes Die Gezeichneten, released in Denmark as Elsker hverandre, from Aage Madelung's novel about pogrom and revolution in the Russian Empire. He casts Jewish refugees, people who left those towns for those reasons, in front of the camera. Berlin in 1922 is full of them. The production company is Primus-Film; no source reached gives the address of the studio, only the city. It is a Danish director's account of Russian antisemitism, shot with Russian survivors on German money, in Germany, in 1922.
suggested_refs: Aage Madelung's novel, source of Die Gezeichneten (1922)
sources: Danish Film Institute, 'Carl Th. Dreyer, Biography (extended)'

stops.name: Hellerup: the studio rented from Benjamin Christensen
stops.date_confidence: [R]: the Hellerup studio rented from Benjamin Christensen appears in the Danish Film Institute extended biography without a date or address; month and day are defaulted to order the segment. Der var engang is attested for 1922 by Dansk Biografisk Leksikon, which also records that the film survives only incompletely.
stops.campa: Back in Denmark he rents studio space at Hellerup from Benjamin Christensen, the director of Haxan, and shoots Der var engang, after Holger Drachmann's fairy play. He has no studio of his own and never will; for forty-five years he works out of other people's buildings, in other people's countries, on other people's money. In what survives of Der var engang, a director is learning to hold a face longer than the story strictly requires. Only fragments survive.
suggested_refs: The surviving fragments of Der var engang (1922), after Holger Drachmann
sources: Danish Film Institute, 'Carl Th. Dreyer, Biography (extended)'

stops.name: Neubabelsberg, Decla-Bioscop: Michael, and Thea von Harbou's pen
stops.date_confidence: premiere date, producer Erich Pommer, cinematographers Karl Freund and Rudolph Mate, and the Harbou co-credit are attested by the English Wikipedia article on Michael (1924 film). Note a correction to an earlier dossier line: the production was Decla-Bioscop, not UFA, whose merger with Decla-Bioscop is dated 1928, so calling the 1924 shoot a UFA production is anachronistic. Coordinate is Studio Babelsberg proper.
stops.campa: At Neubabelsberg he directs Michael for Decla-Bioscop, from Herman Bang's novel of an aging painter and the male model he loves and is ruined by. Erich Pommer produces; Karl Freund and Rudolph Mate are on the cameras. The screenplay he writes with Thea von Harbou, who is married to Fritz Lang and writes everything Lang shoots, so that Dreyer is working inside that circle without any evidence he and Lang were friends. It opens in Berlin on the twenty-sixth of September 1924.
suggested_refs: Herman Bang's novel Mikael (1904), the film's source

stops.name: Valby: Master of the House, and the French offer
stops.date_confidence: the 1925 film, its source in Svend Rindom's play, and the French success that produced the Joan of Arc commission are attested by Dansk Biografisk Leksikon; month and day are defaulted
stops.campa: Du skal aere din Hustru, from Svend Rindom's play, is a domestic film about a household tyrant slowly and methodically disarmed by his old nurse. It is shot small, in rooms, at ordinary human range. In France it is a considerable success, and on the strength of it the Societe Generale des Films offers him a picture of his choosing in Paris. He proposes three subjects: Marie Antoinette, Catherine de' Medici, Joan of Arc. He would say afterward that the choice among them was made by drawing matches.
suggested_refs: Svend Rindom's play, source of Du skal aere din Hustru (1925)
sources: Wikipedia, 'The Passion of Joan of Arc'

stops.name: Paris: a year and a half inside the minutes
stops.date_confidence: the research period and the compression of twenty-nine interrogations over eighteen months into a single day are attested by the English Wikipedia article on the film; the drawing of matches is Dreyer's own claim, reported in the same article, and is tagged [R] accordingly. Month and day defaulted. The Paris coordinate is a city centroid: the sources do not say where he worked, and no visit by Dreyer to Rouen itself is attested anywhere reached.
stops.campa: He spends more than a year and a half in the surviving minutes of the 1431 trial, the interrogations of Joan of Arc written down by clerks who were in the room. Twenty-nine sessions across eighteen months, condensed into one day. He works from the record, question and answer, the way he had worked from court transcripts at Ekstra Bladet. The rights to Joseph Delteil's fashionable 1925 book on Joan have been bought for the production and Delteil is credited on the film. Nothing of his is in it.
suggested_refs: The minutes of the condemnation trial of Joan of Arc, Rouen, 1431
Carl Theodor Dreyer, Four Screenplays (Indiana University Press, 1970), p. 21, on Delteil's uncredited displacement
sources: Wikipedia, 'The Passion of Joan of Arc'
Danish Film Institute, 'La Passion de Jeanne d'Arc'

stops.name: Paris: Falconetti found in a boulevard theatre
stops.date_confidence: attested; the production named is La Garconne, per the English Wikipedia article on Renee Jeanne Falconetti, and the makeup-free screen test the following day is attested there and in the article on the film. Coordinate inherited unchanged from falconetti.journey.json.
stops.campa: He has considered Lillian Gish and Madeleine Renaud. Then he sees Renee Falconetti in an amateur production of La Garconne, a light thing, a comedy, and goes backstage. He is not casting an actress who can play a nineteen-year-old peasant on trial for her life. He is looking for a face that can be photographed for ninety minutes with nothing added to it. The next day, in her apartment near the Champs-Elysees, he asks her to take off her makeup and puts a camera on her bare face.
suggested_refs: The screen tests of Renee Falconetti, November 1926
sources: Wikipedia, 'The Passion of Joan of Arc'

stops.name: Studios de Billancourt: the concrete Rouen
stops.date_confidence: [R] for the set's construction details, which come through the English Wikipedia article on the film; shooting in trial sequence is attested there. Coordinate inherited unchanged from falconetti.journey.json.
stops.campa: Hermann Warm and Jean Hugo build him an entire Rouen at Billancourt, in concrete, the walls ten centimetres thick, painted pink so that panchromatic stock will read them as grey. It is among the most expensive sets standing in Europe that year. He then shoots the trial in sequence, question by question, in the order the clerks recorded it, and puts the camera so close to the faces that the set is barely in the finished film at all. He built a city and then declined to photograph it. Asked later why the close-ups, he answers in terms of the transcript.
stops.quote: There were questions, there were answers- very short, very crisp...Each question, each answer, quite naturally called for a close-up...In addition, the result of the close-ups was that the spectator was as shocked as Joan was, receiving the questions, tortured by them.
stops.quote_source: Dreyer, quoted in John Wakeman, ed., World Film Directors, Volume 1 (H. W. Wilson, 1987), p. 268
suggested_refs: Hermann Warm and Jean Hugo's concrete Rouen at the Studios de Billancourt, 1927
sources: Wikipedia, 'The Passion of Joan of Arc'
Wakeman, ed., World Film Directors, Vol. 1 (1987)

stops.name: Studios de Billancourt: Artaud as the monk Massieu
stops.date_confidence: attested; Antonin Artaud's casting as Jean Massieu is confirmed by the English Wikipedia articles on the film and on Falconetti. Coordinate inherited unchanged from artaud.journey.json. The date is the scene date carried by the two corpus files, not a documented single day of shooting.
stops.campa: Antonin Artaud plays Jean Massieu, the one cleric in the room who bends toward the accused instead of away from her. Dreyer has cast a poet who will spend the rest of his life arguing that the theatre must be cruelty before it is anything else, dressed him in a monk's habit, and asked him to be merciful. Artaud writes about the film afterward, and what he writes concerns the machinery rather than Joan's faith or her voices. On the set he is treated as the rest of them are: the same concrete, the same range, the same lights.
stops.quote: reveal Joan as the victim of one of the most terrible of all perversions: the perversion of a divine principle in its passage through the minds of men, whether they be Church, Government or what you will.
stops.quote_source: Antonin Artaud on the film, quoted in Tom Milne, The Cinema of Carl Dreyer (A. S. Barnes, 1971), pp. 106-107
suggested_refs: Artaud's writings on La Passion de Jeanne d'Arc
sources: Wikipedia, 'The Passion of Joan of Arc'
Milne, The Cinema of Carl Dreyer (1971)

stops.name: Studios de Billancourt: the head shaved on camera
stops.date_confidence: attested that the shaving was written into Falconetti's contract from the start and performed before cast and crew near the end of the shoot; the scene date is inherited from falconetti.journey.json along with the coordinate. The legend of systematic cruelty is [R] and disputed, see the report.
stops.campa: Near the end of the shoot Falconetti's head is shaved in front of the camera and the assembled crew. The clause was in her contract before a foot of film was exposed. She had already knelt on stone through take after take at his direction. Whether what he did to her over these months was method or cruelty is a question her daughter answered one way and the production records answer another, and the argument has run for a century without either side producing a document that closes it. Falconetti never appears in another film.
suggested_refs: Helene Falconetti's family biography, Falconetti, source of the cruelty testimony
sources: Wikipedia, 'The Passion of Joan of Arc'

stops.name: Palads Teatret, Copenhagen: the film comes home first
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Danish Film Institute's page for the film and by the English Wikipedia article; coordinate inherited unchanged from falconetti.journey.json
stops.campa: The French film about the French saint, financed in Paris and shot at Billancourt, opens first in Copenhagen, six months before France is permitted to see it. Dreyer's own city gets it at the Palads Teatret on the twenty-first of April. The delay in Paris is not technical and it is not commercial. It is the archbishop, the government censors, and the nationalist press, who have been objecting since before the first day of shooting to a Danish Protestant laying hands on Joan of Arc at all.
stops.quote: I wanted to interpret a hymn to the triumph of the soul over life.
stops.quote_source: Carl Theodor Dreyer, Danish Film Institute essay on La Passion de Jeanne d'Arc, reprinted by the Criterion Collection
suggested_refs: The Palads Teatret, Copenhagen, site of the world premiere, 21 April 1928
sources: Danish Film Institute, 'La Passion de Jeanne d'Arc'
Wikipedia, 'The Passion of Joan of Arc'

stops.name: Cinema Marivaux, Paris: the archbishop's cuts
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Danish Film Institute's page for the film and the English Wikipedia article, which records both the archbishop's and the government censors' demands for cuts
stops.campa: France finally sees it on the twenty-fifth of October, on the Boulevard des Italiens, in a version the Archbishop of Paris and the government censors have both had their hands in. Church and state examine the film about a girl examined by church and state, and require alterations before it may be shown. The cut that opens on the boulevard is not the cut Dreyer made, which means the reviews that follow are reviews of somebody else's edit. What was taken out, and how much of it, is not recorded in anything reached.
suggested_refs: The censored French release version of La Passion de Jeanne d'Arc, October 1928
sources: Danish Film Institute, 'La Passion de Jeanne d'Arc'
Wikipedia, 'The Passion of Joan of Arc'

stops.name: Berlin: the original negative burns
stops.date_confidence: attested for date and event by the English Wikipedia article, which places the fire at UFA in Berlin. No source reached gives a street address for the laboratory, and the dossier lenses disagreed by some kilometres; the corpus pin from falconetti.journey.json and fritz_lang.journey.json is used unchanged, and the imprecision is stated rather than resolved.
stops.campa: Six weeks after the Paris opening, a fire in the UFA laboratory takes the original camera negative. Everything shot at Billancourt, every take of that face, gone in an afternoon at the same UFA works where Metropolis was built. Dreyer goes back to the alternate takes and assembles a second version out of the material he had rejected. That reconstruction will itself burn, in another fire, some years later. By the mid-1930s the film exists only in prints of prints, degraded copies of a censored cut of a lost original.
suggested_refs: Dreyer's 1929 reconstruction of the Passion from alternate takes, itself later destroyed by fire
sources: Wikipedia, 'The Passion of Joan of Arc'

stops.name: Paris: three years against the Societe Generale des Films
stops.date_confidence: attested by the English Wikipedia article on the film, which states that Dreyer sued the producers for breach of contract over the mutilation of the film and that the lawsuit went on until the fall of 1931, during which he was unable to make another film. The stop is dated to the start of the litigation to keep the segment in travel order; month and day are defaulted. No docket, judgment, or damages figure was located in any source reached, and the outcome is an open gap.
stops.campa: He sues the Societe Generale des Films for breach of contract, accusing the producers of mutilating the film to keep Catholic audiences comfortable. The suit runs until the autumn of 1931. For its whole duration he cannot make a picture; the money will not come to a director who is in court with his last producer. He is forty-two and has directed nine films, one of which no longer exists in the form he shot it. What the court decided, and whether he was paid anything at all, is in no record reached.
suggested_refs: The Dreyer v. Societe Generale des Films breach-of-contract suit, Paris, 1928-1931
sources: Wikipedia, 'The Passion of Joan of Arc'

stops.name: Courtempierre, Loiret: the barn dressed with tombstones
stops.date_confidence: attested by the English Wikipedia article on Vampyr for the location, the April-May 1930 manor scenes, the August churchyard scenes, and the barn dressed with tombstones by Hermann Warm. Note that the Danish Film Institute describes Courtempierre as the fictional village name within the film; the commune is real and the shooting took place in and around it, but no chateau is named by either source. Coordinate corrected to the commune's own.
stops.campa: Nicolas de Gunzburg, a young baron who wants to act, pays for the film and stars in it under the name Julian West. It is his first sound film and he mostly declines to use sound; loosely, very loosely, it comes from Sheridan Le Fanu, and what it resembles is a fever taking place in daylight. They shoot entirely on location around Courtempierre in the Loiret, manor interiors in April and May, churchyard scenes in August. The church is a barn, with tombstones that Hermann Warm has stood in the grass outside it.
stops.quote: Don't you understand that the old book is not a text in the ordinary, stupid sense, but an actor just as much as the others?
stops.quote_source: Dreyer on the storybook pages of Vampyr, quoted in Casper Tybjerg, 'The Ghostly Presence' (visual essay), Criterion Collection DVD, 2008
suggested_refs: Hermann Warm's tombstone-dressed barn at Courtempierre, standing in for the churchyard

stops.name: Berlin: Vampyr booed at its premiere
stops.date_confidence: attested by the English Wikipedia article on Vampyr for the date, the hostile Berlin reception, the Vienna riot demanding refunds, and the September Paris opening on the Boulevard Raspail. The premiere venue is not named in any source reached and the coordinate is city-level.
stops.campa: The Berlin audience boos it. In Vienna the showing produces a riot, the house demanding its money back at the box office. Paris takes it that September on the Boulevard Raspail and is unmoved. The film loses money in every territory that buys it, and forty years pass before there is any wide agreement that it is a masterpiece. Asked at the Berlin premiere what he had been trying to do, he gives the answer he will go on giving for the rest of his life.
stops.quote: I just wanted to make a film different from all other films. I wanted, if you will, to break new ground for the cinema. That is all.
stops.quote_source: Dreyer at the Berlin premiere of Vampyr, quoted in Casper Tybjerg, 'The Rise of the Vampire' (visual essay), Criterion Collection DVD, 2008
suggested_refs: Contemporary Berlin and Vienna press notices of Vampyr, May 1932

stops.name: France: the hospital, while Copenhagen sees the film
stops.date_confidence: attested that Dreyer missed the March 1933 Copenhagen premiere of Vampyr because he had suffered a nervous breakdown and was in a mental hospital in France, per the English Wikipedia article. The city is NOT attested: no source reached names one, and the Paris coordinate here is an explicit placeholder for country-level information. No clinic name and no diagnosis is on record anywhere reached.
stops.campa: Vampyr opens in Copenhagen in March 1933 and its director is not in the house. He is in a mental hospital somewhere in France, after a breakdown. No source reached names the town, the institution, the doctor or the diagnosis. What is on record is the collapse, the year, and the fact that he was not in the house on the night his film opened in his own city. He is forty-four years old. Nine years pass before he completes another film of any length, and ten before he directs another feature.
suggested_refs: The March 1933 Copenhagen premiere of Vampyr, which Dreyer did not attend
sources: Danish Film Institute, 'Carl Th. Dreyer, Biography (extended)'

stops.name: Italian Somaliland: malaria on L'Homme ensable
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Danish Film Institute extended biography, which states that in 1934 Dreyer contracted malaria while attempting to film L'Homme ensable in Italian Somaliland and returned to Denmark unable to complete the project. An earlier dossier line left it open whether he travelled at all; he did. The Mogadishu coordinate is a territory-level proxy, since no filming site is named. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: A year after the hospital he is in East Africa, in the Italian colony, trying to shoot a film called L'Homme ensable. Of all the pictures he did not finish this is the one that leaves the least behind: no footage in circulation, no script in the standard bibliographies, only the title and the territory. The project is abandoned where it stands. He gets malaria and comes home to Denmark with nothing, forty-five years old, unemployed, and carrying a parasite in his blood.
suggested_refs: L'Homme ensable, abandoned 1934 in Italian Somaliland
sources: Danish Film Institute, 'Carl Th. Dreyer, Biography (extended)'

stops.name: Copenhagen, Dansk Kulturfilm: the maternal-aid short
stops.date_confidence: [R] for Moedrehjaelpen specifically, which comes from composite filmographies; the run of commissioned public-information shorts through Denmark's official cultural-film apparatus from 1942 onward is attested by the Danish Film Institute extended biography. Month and day defaulted. Coordinate is a central-Copenhagen placeholder.
stops.campa: After nine years without a camera he takes state work: short commissioned films for the Danish cultural-film apparatus. The first is Moedrehjaelpen, about the institution that helps unmarried and destitute mothers, the machinery that exists in 1942 to keep a woman in Josefina Nielsson's position from having to scrape a match head. A ministry hands him the subject as a job of work. The films are short, instructional, and paid for out of public money, and he will go on making them for years. He is fifty-three. The country is occupied.
suggested_refs: Moedrehjaelpen (Good Mothers, 1942), commissioned short on the Danish maternal-aid institution
sources: Danish Film Institute, 'Carl Th. Dreyer, Biography (extended)'

stops.name: World Cinema, Copenhagen: Vredens Dag in the occupied city
stops.date_confidence: attested; the English Wikipedia article on Day of Wrath names the World Cinema and the date, and records the poor reviews, the complaints about slow pacing, the disappointing box office, and the postwar critical rehabilitation. The cinema's street address is not given in any source reached and the coordinate is a central-Copenhagen placeholder.
stops.campa: Vredens Dag opens at the World Cinema on the thirteenth of November, in a Copenhagen under German occupation. It is a film, from Hans Wiers-Jenssen's play, about a seventeenth-century town that burns an old woman as a witch on evidence extracted under torture, and about the young wife who watches and understands what the machinery can be made to do next. Danish reviewers find it slow. It does poor business. Dreyer denied afterward that he had meant it as an allegory of anything.
suggested_refs: Hans Wiers-Jenssen's play Anne Pedersdotter, source of Vredens Dag

stops.name: Stockholm: the neutral years, and the film he disowned
stops.date_confidence: attested that he left occupied Denmark for Sweden shortly after Day of Wrath's release on the stated pretext of arranging foreign sales, and remained through the war's end. Note a contradiction not resolved here: one fetched source gives the Swedish residency as 1940-1945, the whole occupation, while the composite filmographies tie it to 1943-45. Twa manniskor (1945) is [R] for its production conditions and his repudiation. Month defaulted.
stops.campa: Shortly after Vredens Dag opens he crosses to neutral Sweden, telling the authorities he is going to arrange foreign sales. Friends had advised him to leave. He stays until the war ends. In Stockholm he directs Twa manniskor, from a play by W. O. Somin, under casting and production conditions imposed on him and against his judgment. Afterward he repudiates the picture outright and asks that it be withdrawn from circulation; it is the only one of his films he wanted destroyed. He is still in Stockholm when the occupation ends in May 1945.
suggested_refs: Twa manniskor (1945), from W. O. Somin's play, disowned by its director
sources: Danish Film Institute, 'Carl Th. Dreyer, Biography (extended)'

stops.name: Vedersoe, West Jutland: the murdered priest's parish
stops.date_confidence: attested by the English Wikipedia article on Ordet for the four months of filming, two in studio and two on location at Vedersoe, and for Kaj Munk's parish and his 1944 murder by the Gestapo. Month defaulted within the shooting period. The Vedersoe coordinate is village-level.
stops.campa: He takes the production to Vedersoe in West Jutland, two months on location after two in the studio, because that is where Kaj Munk was parish priest and wrote the play. Munk had been taken out and shot by the Gestapo in January 1944 and left in a ditch. The play is about a farmer's mad son who believes he is Jesus Christ, and about whether a dead woman gets up when he tells her to. Dreyer shoots it in the flat light of the country the author preached in.
stops.quote: there must be harmony between the genuineness of feelings and the genuineness of things.
stops.quote_source: Carl Th. Dreyer, radio interview for New Perspectives on the Arts and Science, 23 October 1950, in Donald Skoller, ed., Dreyer in Double Reflection (Da Capo, 1973), p. 143, quoted in Acquarello, 'Dreyer, Carl Theodor,' Senses of Cinema (2002)
suggested_refs: Kaj Munk's play Ordet (1925), written in the Vedersoe parsonage
sources: Skoller, ed., Dreyer in Double Reflection (1973)
Acquarello, 'Dreyer, Carl Theodor', Senses of Cinema (2002)

stops.name: Dagmar Teatret, Copenhagen: Ordet opens in the house he manages
stops.date_confidence: premiere date and venue attested by the English Wikipedia article on Ordet. The 1952 year for the Dagmar concession is [R], from composite biographies; the award itself and its function as his stable late-life income are attested by the Danish Film Institute extended biography, which calls it his most consequential business appointment.
stops.campa: In 1952 the Danish state handed him the management of the Dagmar cinema in central Copenhagen: a concession, a piece of patronage, and the first income since 1913 that did not depend on somebody agreeing to finance a film. The film he brings there ends with a resurrection played straight, no irony, no dream frame, no explanation afterward, a dead woman sitting up in her coffin because a child asked and a madman told her to. Ordet premieres at the Dagmar on the tenth of January 1955. The proprietor and the director are the same man, which has not happened before in his career and does not happen again.
suggested_refs: The Dagmar Bio concession, awarded by the Danish state, 1952
The Dagmar Teatret, Copenhagen, premiere venue of Ordet, 10 January 1955
sources: Danish Film Institute, 'Carl Th. Dreyer, Biography (extended)'

stops.name: Palazzo del Cinema, Venice Lido: the Golden Lion
stops.date_confidence: attested that Ordet won the Golden Lion at the 16th Venice International Film Festival in 1955; the exact award date is not given in the sources reached and the day is defaulted
stops.campa: Ordet takes the Golden Lion at the sixteenth Venice festival. He is sixty-six, he has been directing for thirty-seven years, and this is the first unambiguous international prize of his life. His previous premiere was booed off a Berlin screen, and most of the 1930s went into short public-information films for a ministry. The effect in Denmark is immediate: the slow, state-supported cinema manager becomes a national possession, to be defended abroad.
suggested_refs: The 16th Venice International Film Festival, 1955

stops.name: British Museum, London: the Jesus who was a Jew
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Danish Film Institute extended biography that Dreyer studied sources at the British Museum for the Jesus project; the dates are broad, spanning the 1950s and 1960s, and month and day are defaulted to order the segment
stops.campa: In the reading rooms of the British Museum he works on the film he will never make. The screenplay is to show Jesus as a practising Jew inside a practising Jewish world, and to place the responsibility for the execution where the Roman occupation and its politics stand rather than on the Jews of Jerusalem. Thirty years earlier he spent eighteen months in the minutes of one heresy proceeding. He is now reading the sources for another. No year is recorded for the work beyond the 1950s and the 1960s.
suggested_refs: Dreyer's research notebooks for the unrealized Jesus of Nazareth
sources: Danish Film Institute, 'Carl Th. Dreyer, Biography (extended)'

stops.name: Jerusalem: Hebrew, and the locations he never shot
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Danish Film Institute extended biography that he travelled to Israel for the Jesus project and taught himself Hebrew; no year is given for the journey and 1958 is chosen only to order the segment, with month and day defaulted
stops.campa: He goes to Israel, scouts locations, and teaches himself Hebrew in his sixties so that the dialogue can be checked against the language it would have been spoken in. It is what he went to Maihaugen for with a medieval church, and to Vedersoe for with a dead priest's parish: the genuineness of things set next to the genuineness of feelings. He has not directed a feature since Ordet. No year is on record for the journey, and the film is never financed.
suggested_refs: Dreyer's location survey in Israel for Jesus of Nazareth
sources: Danish Film Institute, 'Carl Th. Dreyer, Biography (extended)'

stops.name: Copenhagen: Om filmen, and the royal medal
stops.date_confidence: [R] for Om filmen's 1959 Copenhagen publication, which comes from standard bibliographies and is corroborated by Danish Wikipedia's listing of it as a collection of articles, statements, and interviews. The Ingenio et Arti medal of 1963 is attested by Dansk Biografisk Leksikon and is mentioned here rather than given its own stop. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Om filmen appears in Copenhagen: not a treatise but a gathering, his articles, statements, and interviews put between covers. Four years later the crown gives him the Ingenio et Arti medal. He is being canonized in his own country while he still cannot get a film financed, which is the ordinary Danish arrangement. In 1964 the screenplays of four of the major films are collected as Fire film. Asked in these years what he is after in the work, he puts technique second and says what comes before it.
stops.quote: What interests me—and this comes before technique—is reproducing the feelings of the characters in my films...The important thing...is not only to catch hold of the words they say, but also the thoughts behind the words.
stops.quote_source: Dreyer, quoted in David Thomson, The New Biographical Dictionary of Film, 5th ed. (Knopf, 2010), p. 286
suggested_refs: Om filmen (Copenhagen, 1959)
Fire film (1964), the collected screenplays of four major works
sources: Thomson, The New Biographical Dictionary of Film (2010)

stops.name: Nordisk Film, Valby: the last film, in the first studio
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Danish Film Institute extended biography that Gertrud was shot at the Nordisk Film studio complex at Valby in 1964; month and day are defaulted
stops.campa: He shoots Gertrud, from Hjalmar Soederberg's play, with Nina Pens Rode, in the same Valby studio where he was hired to read other men's scenarios in 1913. Fifty-one years in the same buildings. The film is about a woman who will not accept less than everything from love and therefore ends alone, and it is shot in long takes in which people sit side by side and speak past each other without looking. He is seventy-five and it is the last thing he finishes.
stops.quote: Gertrud is a film I made with all my heart.
stops.quote_source: Dreyer, quoted in David Thomson, The New Biographical Dictionary of Film, 5th ed. (Knopf, 2010), p. 286
suggested_refs: Hjalmar Soederberg's play Gertrud (1906), the film's source
sources: Danish Film Institute, 'Carl Th. Dreyer, Biography (extended)'
Thomson, The New Biographical Dictionary of Film (2010)

stops.name: Le Studio Medicis, Paris: the reels out of order
stops.date_confidence: attested by the English Wikipedia article on Gertrud for the date, the venue, and the catalogue of failures: equipment breakdowns, poor subtitles, reels projected out of order, and a hostile house. The rue Champollion coordinate for Le Studio Medicis is an approximation, not confirmed by the fetched source.
stops.campa: Gertrud opens in Paris on the eighteenth of December and the screening comes apart. The equipment fails. The subtitles are bad. The reels are run out of order. The audience, watching a film composed almost entirely of people sitting still and talking, delivered to them scrambled, turns on it. Thirty-six years earlier this city had argued for a year about whether a Danish Protestant was fit to touch Joan of Arc. It is the premiere of his last film.
suggested_refs: Le Studio Medicis, rue Champollion, Paris, site of the Gertrud premiere

stops.name: Venice: half the house walks out, the other half stands
stops.date_confidence: attested by the English Wikipedia article on Gertrud that the film was booed at Cannes in 1965 and that at a Venice screening more than half the audience walked out while the remainder gave a standing ovation that visibly moved Dreyer. The Venice screening's exact date is not given and the day is defaulted; the Cannes reception is named in the confidence field rather than staged as a stop, since the two events are separate.
stops.campa: At Venice more than half the audience gets up and leaves during the film. The ones who stay to the end stand and applaud, and Dreyer, who is seventy-six and has been booed in Berlin and in Vienna and jeered at Cannes earlier the same year, is visibly moved in front of them. It is the same room, the same evening, the same film. It is also the last festival showing of a new Dreyer picture in his lifetime; he does not direct again. What he said to anyone on the way out of the hall that night is not recorded anywhere reached.
suggested_refs: The 1965 Cannes and Venice screenings of Gertrud

stops.name: Copenhagen: three million kroner, one tenth of a budget
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Danish Film Institute extended biography that in 1967 the Danish Ministry of Culture allocated three million kroner, one tenth of the estimated budget, to the Jesus film. Month and day defaulted. The claim, carried by earlier dossiers, that he corresponded with the American producer Blevins Davis for sixteen years appears in no source reached and is left out. The Medea screenplay written with Elsa Gress is [R], from standard bibliographies only.
stops.campa: The Danish Ministry of Culture puts up three million kroner for the Jesus film. The budget is estimated at thirty. He is seventy-eight, he has been working on this screenplay since before the war, he has the language, the locations, and the research, and the state has given him a tenth of what it costs. The rest of the money does not come from anywhere else. He also has an unrealized Medea, written with Elsa Gress, and he does not shoot that either. Two screenplays sit finished on his desk with no production behind either of them.
suggested_refs: The Danish Ministry of Culture's 1967 allocation toward Jesus of Nazareth
sources: Danish Film Institute, 'Carl Th. Dreyer, Biography (extended)'

stops.name: Dalgas Boulevard, Frederiksberg: pneumonia
stops.date_confidence: attested; the date is given by Dansk Biografisk Leksikon, which localises the death to Frederiksberg (Lindevang), the parish containing Dalgas Boulevard, and pneumonia is stated both by the Danish Film Institute extended biography and by the English Wikipedia article. An earlier dossier treated the cause as contested between sources; on two independent sources it is not. The thirty-year residence on Dalgas Boulevard is attested by the Danish Film Institute.
stops.campa: He dies on the twentieth of March, seventy-nine years old, of pneumonia, in the Lindevang parish of Frederiksberg where he has lived for some thirty years in a modest apartment on Dalgas Boulevard. Ebba, whom he married in 1911, survives him. He has not directed since Gertrud, four years earlier. Frederiksberg is where his adoptive parents sent him to school in 1904 and where he dies in 1968, a few streets apart. He leaves an unmade Jesus film with a tenth of its money in hand, an unmade Medea, and fourteen features made across half a century.
suggested_refs: The apartment on Dalgas Boulevard, Frederiksberg, Dreyer's home from about 1938
sources: Danish Film Institute, 'Carl Th. Dreyer, Biography (extended)'

stops.name: Frederiksberg AEldre Kirkegaard: a modest grave
stops.date_confidence: burial at Frederiksberg AEldre Kirkegaard is attested by Dansk Biografisk Leksikon, by Danish Wikipedia, and by the English Wikipedia article on the cemetery, which lists him among its burials. The exact date of interment is not given in any source reached and the day is a placeholder after the death. The plot within the cemetery was not located. Coordinate from the cemetery's own Wikipedia page.
stops.campa: He is buried behind Frederiksberg Church, in the old cemetery laid out in 1734, about a kilometre east of the apartment on Dalgas Boulevard. The plot is not recorded in anything reachable, and neither is the date of the interment; Dansk Biografisk Leksikon, Danish Wikipedia and the cemetery's own list of burials give the ground and nothing finer. His own institute's biography, describing the grave, puts it in the same sentence as his sitting room.
stops.quote: Carl Th. Dreyer was a modest man, as were his sitting room and, later, his grave.
stops.quote_source: Danish Film Institute, 'Carl Th. Dreyer, Biography (extended)'
suggested_refs: Frederiksberg AEldre Kirkegaard, established 1734 behind Frederiksberg Church
sources: Danish Film Institute, 'Carl Th. Dreyer, Biography (extended)'

stops.name: Copenhagen, Gyldendal: Jesus fra Nazaret goes to press
stops.date_confidence: publication of Jesus fra Nazaret: Et filmmanuskript by Gyldendal in 1968 is attested by Danish Wikipedia's bibliography; the month is not given and is defaulted to place it after his death in March of the same year. The Copenhagen coordinate is the publisher's city, not a located address.
stops.campa: In the year of his death Gyldendal prints the screenplay as a book: Jesus fra Nazaret, et filmmanuskript. Decades of reading, the Hebrew he taught himself in his sixties, the Israeli locations and the three million kroner that were a tenth of what was needed come out as a text with stage directions and no film attached to them. It is the last thing he publishes and the only form the project takes. Forty years earlier he had begun from a document of the same kind, the minutes of a trial, and made a film out of it.
suggested_refs: Carl Th. Dreyer, Jesus fra Nazaret: Et filmmanuskript (Copenhagen: Gyldendal, 1968)
sources: Danish Film Institute, 'Carl Th. Dreyer, Biography (extended)'
